title: API Versioning Strategies
description: Compare common API versioning approaches, including URI, header, and query-parameter strategies, and learn how to evolve your API without breaking existing clients.

data.text: APIs change over time. New features, breaking schema changes, and deprecations are inevitable. Versioning gives consumers control over when they adopt changes and lets providers evolve without forcing every client to update at once. Choosing a versioning strategy early saves migration headaches later and demonstrates maturity in your API design process. Without versioning, even small changes can trigger a cascade of production failures across unknown clients that you may never discover until your monitoring pages light up.

Without versioning, a single breaking change can break every integration simultaneously. Versioning isolates change, communicates intent, and provides a migration path. It also makes it easier to document and test each release of your API independently. When versioning is done well, teams can ship new features in v2 while supporting v1 clients with minimal extra effort. This separation of concerns is essential for platforms with many external integrations, partner ecosystems, or mobile apps distributed through app stores where updates cannot be forced.

data.title: Breaking Changes
data.text: Removing a required field, renaming an endpoint, changing a response type, or altering authentication rules are all breaking changes. Minor additions and bug fixes are usually backward compatible and do not require a version bump.

URI versioning places the version number directly in the URL path, such as /v1/users or /v2/users. It is the most visible and commonly used strategy. Clients see the version immediately, which simplifies routing and caching. The main criticism is that it violates the principle that a URI should uniquely identify a resource, since /v1/users and /v2/users describe the same conceptual resource. Despite this theoretical concern, URI versioning remains the industry standard because its visibility and operational simplicity outweigh the purity argument for most engineering teams.

data.text: Header versioning sends the version in a custom header such as X-API-Version. It keeps URIs clean and aligns with REST purist views, but it is invisible to developers testing with a browser. Query-parameter versioning uses ?version=1, which is easy to test but can cause caching issues because query strings are often included in cache keys. Each approach has trade-offs between visibility, testability, and cache friendliness, so the right choice depends on who your primary clients are and how you monitor traffic.

data.title: Keep these rules in mind
items: Deprecate old versions with a clear timeline and communicate it to consumers.
Return the API version in response headers so clients can programmatically detect it.
Avoid versioning every small change; reserve versions for breaking changes.
Support only the current and immediately previous version to limit maintenance cost.

items.question: Can I mix versioning strategies?
items.answer: It is possible but not recommended. Mixed strategies confuse clients and increase testing complexity. Choose one approach and apply it consistently.

items.question: What if I need to support many versions?
items.answer: Supporting too many versions increases maintenance burden. Limit active support to one or two versions and retire older versions on a regular schedule.

data.title: Takeaway
points: Versioning protects clients from unexpected breaking changes.
URI versioning is the most visible and widely adopted approach.
Deprecation and clear communication are as important as the versioning scheme itself.
data.takeaway: A thoughtful versioning strategy lets your API grow without breaking the integrations that depend on it.
